q7.answer: Each migration runs in its own transaction, so the failed one rolls back, but migrations that already committed stay applied. They are additive, so the live release is unaffected. The deploy stops, the new release is never started, the live colour keeps serving, and the run pages naming the failed migration. The next deploy's steps 4 and 5 see only the unrecorded migrations.

q8.answer: The run reads the listener fresh each time, and the listener is the only authority for which colour is live. The new colour is simply the opposite one. Target group tags (status, release, switched_at) record the state, but step 3 treats the tags only as a sanity check against the listener and stops and pages if they disagree.

q9.answer: A pipeline concurrency group lock named catalog-web-deploy prevents overlap. A run takes it at step 1 and holds it through step 14, including the full 30-minute hold of the old colour, so about 40 to 50 minutes. A waiting run is replaced by a newer merge.

q10.answer: The pipeline job health-checks and smoke-tests the 4 new instances directly at their private addresses, never through the listener, so the new release gets no public traffic until the switch. Whether the pipeline runner can actually reach those private addresses is assumed, not verified, and is listed as open.

q11.answer: Step 5 of the pipeline runs the new release's migration bundle, before any new instance starts. The migration tool's database lock, assumed to be a session-scoped PostgreSQL advisory lock, stops two runs migrating at once, and its own table of applied migrations means each migration is run only once. The tool itself is not chosen, and the lock behaviour is an unverified assumption.

q12.answer: They are stopped. After an abort the 4 new instances are deregistered and stopped, and the group is tagged failed. After a rollback the failed colour's instances are stopped and it is tagged rolled_back, so it cannot be inspected, although its logs and metrics stay. The next deploy treats that colour as new, because it is the opposite of the listener. Step 3 ignores its tags, stops any stray instances and requires 0, and step 6 overwrites its tags.
